title: How to choose an ergonomic office chair
sub: Before you look at brands, measure and check five things.
text: How to choose an ergonomic office chair Before you look at brands, measure and check five things. An ergonomic chair is not one labelled “ergonomic”. It is one that adjusts to your body. That simple definition changes the order of work: measurements first, brands second. Check seat height The goal is for your feet to rest fully on the floor or a footrest, with your thighs roughly level. Measure the seat-height range against your height. On chairs such as the Aeron, this is tied to choosing size A, B or C. Take seat depth seriously When you lean fully against the back, the seat edge should not press behind your knees. If depth is not adjustable, check its dimensions against your thigh length. Lumbar support The back should preserve your spine’s natural curve. Check whether the lumbar support moves or stays fixed, and whether its firmness adjusts. This often depends on the purchased configuration, not just the model. Arms Arms should hold your forearms without lifting your shoulders, and should not stop you getting close to the desk. Height matters most, followed by width and depth. Before buying Compare the weight capacity with your weight. Choose casters to suit your floor. Read the seller’s return and warranty terms. If possible, sit in the chair for a few hours first. Being expensive does not by itself make a chair suitable. Choose one whose adjustment range fits your body, then take time to set it up properly once it arrives.

title: Where to start with ergonomic workspace equipment
sub: A sensible buying order, beginning with what affects your body most.
text: Where to start with ergonomic workspace equipment A sensible buying order, beginning with what affects your body most. You do not need to buy everything at once. A simple order usually helps you spend sensibly, and shows you which change really helped. 1. First, adjust what you own Before any purchase, adjust your current chair, screen height and keyboard position. Sometimes a laptop on a few books and a separate keyboard solves part of the problem today. 2. The screen If you work on a laptop, a stand with a separate keyboard is a big change. If you have a monitor, an arm also frees up desk surface as well as setting the height. 3. The chair A chair is usually the largest expense. It makes sense if you sit for hours a day, but read a chair guide before buying. 4. The standing desk An adjustable desk lets you change position through the day. The goal is not to stand all day. It is to avoid staying in one position for a long time. 5. The details A keyboard and mouse, if your wrists tire after work. Proper lighting, if you work into the evening. A footrest, if your feet do not reach the floor comfortably.

title: How to build a dual-monitor workspace
sub: How you arrange screens affects your neck more than how many you have.
text: How to build a dual-monitor workspace How you arrange screens affects your neck more than how many you have. Two monitors can make work easier, but a poor arrangement keeps turning your neck to one side. Before buying, decide how you will use both screens. Using both equally? Place the two screens side by side with the join directly in front of you, and angle the outer edges slightly toward you. Is one the main screen? Put the main screen straight in front of you and the secondary one beside it. This keeps your neck straight for most of the time. Height and distance Set the top of the screen at or slightly below eye level, at about arm’s length. If you wear multifocal glasses, you will probably need to lower the screen. Choosing an arm Check each monitor’s weight without its stand. Find the VESA pattern on the back of the monitor. Measure your desk-edge thickness for the clamp. Compare the total width of both screens with your desk. If your monitors differ, match their brightness and the height of their top edges, so your eyes tire less when moving between them.

title: Monitor arm vs. monitor stand
sub: An arm is not always better. In these cases a simple stand is enough.
text: Monitor arm vs. monitor stand An arm is not always better. In these cases a simple stand is enough. Both raise the screen, but they differ in adjustability, installation and cost. When is a stand enough? Only one person uses the monitor and its position does not change. The monitor’s own stand gives the right height. Your desk edge does not suit a clamp. Your budget is limited. When is an arm worth it? You move between sitting and standing through the day. Your desk is small and you want clear space under the screen. You have two monitors and want to align them precisely. You sometimes turn the screen toward a colleague or guest. Three measurements before buying an arm The monitor’s weight without its stand must be within the arm’s capacity. The monitor needs a VESA pattern. And the desk needs a suitable thickness and edge for a clamp or grommet; thin or glass tops can cause problems. Permitted screen size alone is not enough. Two monitors of the same size can differ greatly in weight, especially ultrawide and curved models.

title: How to choose a laptop stand
sub: Fixed or folding? It depends on where your laptop lives.
text: How to choose a laptop stand Fixed or folding? It depends on where your laptop lives. A laptop’s core problem is that its screen and keyboard are joined. Raise the screen and the keyboard sits too high for typing. Place the keyboard well and your neck bends down. A stand only fully works with a separate keyboard and mouse. Fixed stands They suit a permanent desk. They are stable and simply built, but they have no height adjustment, so check the height against your stature and desk. The mStand is an example. Folding stands They suit travel, cafés and shared offices. They are light and have several heights, but usually feel less stable when you touch the screen. The Roost is an example. What to check Does the final height bring the top of the screen near eye level? Are your laptop’s size and weight supported? Does it leave the laptop’s vents clear? Do you have a separate keyboard and mouse?

title: Ergonomics for home offices
sub: A simple checklist for turning a table at home into a real workspace.
text: Ergonomics for home offices A simple checklist for turning a table at home into a real workspace. At home we often work on things not made for work: a dining table, a sofa or the edge of a bed. Before any purchase, apply the simple principles. Adjust from the bottom up Feet: flat on the floor or a footrest. Thighs: roughly level. Lower back: supported by the backrest. Shoulders: relaxed, not lifted. Elbows: close to your body. Wrists: nearly straight. Screen: its top at or slightly below eye level. Table too high? Raise the seat until your elbows are level with the keyboard, and use a footrest if your feet leave the floor. This is a simple way to work at a dining table. Change your position Even the best position gets tiring if it stays unchanged for hours. Build in short breaks to get up, walk and look into the distance. Do not forget light Place the screen so that a window is not directly behind or in front of it. A window to the side usually gives less glare, and evening lighting should light the room as well as the screen. When to buy a standing desk If you work several hours a day and have a fixed space, an adjustable desk is worth considering. Before buying, check its lowest and highest heights with the Body Fit Calculator.

title: Workspace accessories worth considering
sub: One question for each item: exactly what problem does it solve?
text: Workspace accessories worth considering One question for each item: exactly what problem does it solve? Accessory buying easily gets out of hand. Before buying, ask what specific problem the item solves. If you cannot answer, you probably do not need it. Monitor-top light If you work into the evening and your desk surface is dark, this type of light gives light without occupying the desk. Check your monitor’s edge thickness against its specifications. Footrest If your feet leave the floor once your seat height is right, a footrest solves it. If your feet rest comfortably, you do not need one. Cable management Under-desk trays and cable ties are cheap and make an adjustable desk safer, as cables do not get pulled when the height changes. What can wait Repeated decorative items. Risers that do not suit your desk’s dimensions. Several items bought for the same single problem.

title: How to sit properly at your desk
sub: A neutral posture from feet to eyes, and why the best posture is the next one.
text: How to sit properly at your desk A neutral posture from feet to eyes, and why the best posture is the next one. “Sit up straight” is advice everyone has heard, but few people know what straight actually means. OSHA’s guide to computer workstations uses the term “neutral posture”: a position in which your joints are naturally aligned and muscles and tendons carry the least strain.  Start at the bottom: feet Your feet should rest fully on the floor. If they do not reach once the chair height is right, a footrest solves it. Your thighs should be roughly parallel to the floor and your knees about level with your hips, with your feet slightly forward of your knees. Hips and back Sit all the way back so the backrest can support your lower back. Your torso and neck should be roughly vertical and in line. You do not need to sit rigidly upright: leaning back a little is perfectly fine if the backrest supports you well. Shoulders, elbows and wrists Let your shoulders relax and keep your elbows close to your body. OSHA suggests an elbow angle between 90 and 120 degrees. Hands, wrists and forearms should be straight, in line and roughly parallel to the floor. If you lift your shoulders to reach the keyboard, the desk or keyboard is too high for you. Head and eyes Your head should balance on your neck, not jut forward. If you lean towards the screen, it is usually too far away, too low, or the text is too small. We cover screen distance and height in a separate monitor guide. The best posture is the next one Even the best posture becomes tiring if held for hours. Cornell University’s ergonomics guidance stresses changing position every 20 to 30 minutes and moving for a couple of minutes. Simply standing is not enough; movement is what matters. A quick check Feet rest fully on the floor or a footrest. Thighs are roughly level and the seat edge does not press behind your knees. Your lower back rests against the backrest. Shoulders are relaxed and elbows stay by your sides. Wrists are straight, not bent up or down. You can see the screen without bending your head.

title: How far away and how high should your monitor be?
sub: 50 to 100 cm away, the top of the screen at or below eye level, and a few exceptions.
text: How far away and how high should your monitor be? 50 to 100 cm away, the top of the screen at or below eye level, and a few exceptions. Where your monitor sits directly affects your neck, shoulders and eyes. A screen that is too low bends your head forward, one that is too high tips your neck back, and one that is too close makes your eyes work harder. Fortunately, a few simple rules solve most cases.  Distance: about an arm’s length OSHA’s guidance is to place the monitor at least 50 cm (20 inches) from your eyes, with a preferred distance of 50 to 100 cm. The American Academy of Ophthalmology suggests about 25 inches, roughly an arm’s length. The real test is whether you can read all the text with your head and torso upright and your back supported. If the text is hard to read at that distance, make it larger in your system settings rather than pulling the screen closer. A screen that is too close makes your eyes work harder to converge. Height: top of the screen at or below eye level The top line of text should be at or slightly below eye level, so your gaze falls slightly downward. This is what both OSHA and the American Academy of Ophthalmology recommend. Straight in front of you Put your main monitor directly in front of you, in line with the keyboard. A screen off to one side keeps your neck twisted for hours. For two screens, see our dual-monitor guide. Light and reflections OSHA suggests placing the monitor at right angles to windows, so daylight neither falls on the screen nor into your eyes. Match the screen brightness to the light around you. When the height will not work If the monitor stand is not tall enough, a monitor arm or even a few sturdy books helps. If you wear bifocal or progressive lenses, you may need the screen lower so you do not tip your head back. For a laptop, a laptop stand with a separate keyboard and mouse is the main fix.

title: What is the right desk height?
sub: Find your desk height from your own elbows, not from a store chart.
text: What is the right desk height? Find your desk height from your own elbows, not from a store chart. Standard desks have a fixed height designed for an “average person”, but nobody is exactly average. The good news is that you do not need to memorise a number: your body is the measuring stick.  The elbow rule First set your chair so your feet rest on the floor and your thighs are roughly level. Then relax your shoulders and bend your elbows. The surface your hands work on, meaning the keyboard and mouse, should be close to that height or slightly below, so your forearms stay roughly parallel to the floor. If your desk is fixed and too high This is the most common problem. Raise the chair until your elbows are level with the desk, then add a footrest so your feet are not left dangling. Another option is an under-desk keyboard tray. Cornell University’s guidance favours a tray that tilts the keyboard slightly away from you (negative tilt). If your desk is too low A low desk pulls your shoulders forward and bends your back. Sturdy desk risers or a different desk are the fix. Do not lower the chair so far that your knees rise above your hips. For a standing desk The same rule applies when standing: forearms roughly parallel to the floor and shoulders relaxed. So a standing desk needs a height range that covers both your seated and your standing elbow height. The site’s Body Fit Calculator gives a rough starting point from your height. In short Measure desk height against your own elbows, not a standard figure. Desk too high: raise the chair and add a footrest. Desk too low: sturdy risers or a different desk. Standing desk: compare its height range with your seated and standing elbow heights.

title: Where to put your keyboard and mouse to spare your wrists
sub: The right distance, height and angle for keyboard and mouse, and a common mistake with keyboard feet.
text: Where to put your keyboard and mouse to spare your wrists The right distance, height and angle for keyboard and mouse, and a common mistake with keyboard feet. For most of your computer hours, your hands are on the keyboard and mouse. Moving these two by a few centimetres can be the difference between tired wrists and comfortable ones.  Close and centred Place the keyboard directly in front of you, with the middle of the letter keys (around H and J) in line with your navel. Keep it close enough that your elbows stay at your sides and you do not have to reach. Height: level with your elbows According to OSHA, hands, wrists and forearms should be straight, in line and roughly parallel to the floor. If the keyboard is above elbow height your shoulders rise; if it is far below, your wrists bend upward. Leave the keyboard feet folded Many keyboards have two small feet at the back that tilt the keyboard towards you. That tilt usually bends your wrists further upward. Cornell University’s guidance goes the other way and suggests a slight negative tilt, with the keyboard sloping gently away from you, for example on a negative-tilt keyboard tray. Without such a tray, at least keep the keyboard flat. Mouse: beside the keyboard, at the same level Place the mouse right next to the keyboard and at the same height. If you have to reach for it, a keyboard without a number pad brings the mouse closer. Move it from your forearm rather than only from your wrist. Palm rests A soft rest in front of the keyboard is for resting between bursts of typing. While typing, it is better for your hands to move freely without your wrists pressing on the edge. Never rest your wrists on a hard desk edge. A quick check The keyboard is centred and close. Elbows are at your sides and forearms roughly level. The keyboard is flat or tilted slightly away, not towards you. The mouse is beside the keyboard at the same height. Your wrists are not on a hard desk edge.

title: How to use a standing desk: how long to stand and sit
sub: A standing desk is not for standing all day. A simple pattern for switching between sitting, standing and moving.
text: How to use a standing desk: how long to stand and sit A standing desk is not for standing all day. A simple pattern for switching between sitting, standing and moving. After buying a standing desk, many people either stand all day and get tired, or stop raising it after a few weeks. Both miss the real point: changing your body’s position regularly.  Standing does not replace sitting Standing for a long time holds your body in one position, just like sitting for a long time. Cornell’s guidance says plainly that simply standing is insufficient: what matters is changing posture and moving. A simple pattern Cornell suggests this: in each half hour, sit for about 20 minutes in a good posture, stand for about 8 minutes and move for about 2 minutes. They also stress that the exact numbers are not critical; what matters is changing position roughly every 20 to 30 minutes and moving for a couple of minutes. Start gently If you are not used to standing, begin with short periods and build up. Comfortable shoes and an anti-fatigue mat make standing easier. If you have foot or back pain, talk to a professional before changing your routine. The right height in both positions When you raise the desk, the elbow rule still applies: forearms roughly parallel to the floor and shoulders relaxed. Check the monitor height too; if it is on an arm, you may need to adjust it as well. Make the habit easy Save your sitting and standing heights in the desk’s memory presets. Take short tasks such as phone calls or email standing up. Set a simple reminder on your phone or computer. Use the two minutes of movement to actually walk: refill your water or do a few stretches.

title: Screen eye strain: causes and simple fixes
sub: Blinking less, poor lighting and the wrong distance, plus a simple reminder called 20-20-20.
text: Screen eye strain: causes and simple fixes Blinking less, poor lighting and the wrong distance, plus a simple reminder called 20-20-20. If your eyes feel dry, tired or blurry after a few hours at a computer, you are not alone. The American Academy of Ophthalmology explains that looking at screens for long periods does not permanently damage your eyes, but it can cause temporary strain, dryness and blur. The good news is that most causes have simple fixes.  Blink According to the American Academy of Ophthalmology, we normally blink about 15 times a minute, but only about 5 to 7 times a minute while using screens. Blinking keeps the surface of the eye moist. Make a conscious effort to blink more; even a small note beside the screen helps. Look into the distance Every so often, look up from the screen at something far away. A common reminder is “20-20-20”: every 20 minutes, look at something about 20 feet (6 m) away for about 20 seconds. A window is ideal. Brightness and contrast If your screen is much brighter than its surroundings, your eyes work harder. Match the screen brightness to the room and raise the contrast if needed. A bright screen in a dark room is tiring; a soft light on the desk helps. Reduce reflections Daylight or lamp light reflecting on the screen tires your eyes. Place the screen at right angles to windows, and if glare persists, a matte screen filter is another option. Distance and angle Keep the screen about an arm’s length away, with your gaze slightly downward. Our monitor distance and height guide covers this in more detail. When to see a doctor If your eyes are constantly red, blurry or watery, become sensitive to light or hurt, see an eye doctor. If you wear glasses, ask whether lenses for computer distance would help you.

title: A few simple stretches at your desk
sub: Three gentle moves for neck, shoulders and upper body that fit into your two minutes of movement.
text: A few simple stretches at your desk Three gentle moves for neck, shoulders and upper body that fit into your two minutes of movement. Short movement breaks are an important part of healthy desk work. Cornell University’s guidance suggests changing position roughly every 20 to 30 minutes and moving for a couple of minutes. You can do these three simple moves in those breaks. Before you start: these moves should be gentle and painless. Never push into pain. If you have an injury, recent surgery or ongoing pain, check with a doctor or physiotherapist first.  1. Gentle neck tilt Sit or stand tall with relaxed shoulders. Slowly tilt your head to one side, bringing your ear towards your shoulder without lifting the shoulder. Stay for a few slow breaths, then do the other side. 2. Overhead reach Stand up, interlace your fingers and slowly raise your arms overhead with your palms facing the ceiling. Lengthen your body a little, hold for a few breaths and lower slowly. It feels good after a long time leaning forward. 3. Shoulder-blade squeeze Bend your elbows and keep them by your sides. Gently draw your shoulder blades together and slightly down, opening your chest. Hold for a few seconds and release. Repeat a few times. Most important of all: walk No stretch replaces walking. Get up, refill your water, go to the window and look into the distance; your eyes get a rest too. Keep every move gentle and painless. Do not hold your breath. Do not bounce or force a stretch. Stop if anything hurts.

title: Working on a laptop for hours without neck pain
sub: A laptop’s core problem is that screen and keyboard are joined. The fix is simple.
text: Working on a laptop for hours without neck pain A laptop’s core problem is that screen and keyboard are joined. The fix is simple. A laptop is built for portability, not for eight hours at a desk. Cornell University’s guidance sums up the problem: with a laptop, the screen and keyboard are not separate. If the screen is at the right height, the keyboard is too high; if the keyboard is right, the screen is too low.  What a laptop on the desk does With the laptop flat on the desk, the screen sits well below eye level and your head bends to see it. Your neck then holds the weight of your head in that position for hours. The fix: screen up, hands down For sustained use, Cornell recommends a separate keyboard. Put the laptop on a stand so the top of the screen comes close to eye level, and work with a separate keyboard and mouse on the desk. The laptop effectively becomes a monitor. Fixed or folding stand? Fixed stands, such as a single piece of bent aluminium, are solid and simple on a desk. Folding stands are light and fit in a bag, which matters if you move between home and office. Check whether the height is adjustable too; a fixed-height stand may not be tall enough for you. If you do not have a stand yet A few sturdy books or a box, together with any separate keyboard and mouse you own, makes a difference today. Just make sure the laptop is stable and its vents are not blocked. Travel and short sessions For short tasks it is fine to use the laptop directly; just take your breaks. Avoid working with the laptop on your lap: your head bends and your hands have nowhere good to go. A folding stand and a compact keyboard in your bag make a temporary office bearable.

title: Workspace lighting: windows, lamps and screen glare
sub: Where the monitor sits relative to the window, enough light on the desk, and ways to cut glare.
text: Workspace lighting: windows, lamps and screen glare Where the monitor sits relative to the window, enough light on the desk, and ways to cut glare. Good lighting does not simply mean more light. A screen showing the window’s reflection and a room lit only by the screen both tire your eyes.  Window to the side, not behind or in front OSHA recommends placing the monitor at right angles to windows. With a window behind you, it reflects on the screen; with a window behind the screen, bright light shines straight into your eyes, which keep adjusting between the screen and the bright window. If you cannot move the desk, curtains or blinds help. Match screen brightness to the room According to the American Academy of Ophthalmology, a screen brighter than its surroundings makes your eyes work harder. Turn the brightness up by day and down at night. Many systems can do this automatically. Light on the desk, not on the screen When you work into the evening, you need a soft light on the desk. Place a lamp so it lights paper and keyboard but does not show in the screen. Monitor light bars are made for exactly this: they light the desk surface and are designed not to reflect on the screen. Before buying, check the specifications and that it fits your monitor’s thickness and curve. Ceiling lights A ceiling light directly behind you may show in the screen. If it does, tilt the screen slightly or use indirect light. When glare persists Change the screen’s vertical tilt slightly. Try a matte filter on a glossy screen. Move the light source, not your head.

title: Set up your ergonomic chair in six steps
sub: Even the most expensive chair will not help if it is not adjusted. The right order, from height to headrest.
text: Set up your ergonomic chair in six steps Even the most expensive chair will not help if it is not adjusted. The right order, from height to headrest. An ergonomic chair arrives with factory settings, not your body’s settings. Many people never try the levers. Follow these six steps in order, because each one affects the next.  1. Seat height Stand in front of the chair and set the seat at about the bottom of your kneecap. Then sit: your feet should rest fully on the floor, thighs roughly level and knees about level with your hips. If your desk is fixed and high, set the chair to suit the desk and add a footrest. 2. Seat depth Sit all the way back. A small gap should remain between the front edge of the seat and the back of your knees, usually a few fingers’ width. If the seat edge presses behind your knees, slide the seat back. 3. Lumbar support The lumbar support should sit in the natural curve of your lower back, neither higher nor lower. If its height or depth adjusts, find the position that feels supportive without pushing. 4. Back angle and tension Set the back tension so you can lean back slightly and the backrest holds you without effort. If it has a recline lock, you do not have to lock it fully upright; many people are more comfortable leaning back a little. 5. Armrests Lower the armrests until your shoulders do not lift, and raise them enough for your forearms to rest on them. Aim for an elbow angle between 90 and 120 degrees. If the arms stop you getting close to the desk, lower them or move them aside. 6. Headrest, if there is one A headrest is for when you lean back, not for pushing your head forward while typing. Set it behind the lower part of your head. After the chair Now match the desk, keyboard and monitor to the chair. The desk height and monitor distance guides are the next steps. New settings can feel strange for the first few days; if you are still uncomfortable after a week, adjust again.

title: Standing desk buying guide: seven things to check
sub: Height range, motors, stability, capacity and a few details that store photos do not show.
text: Standing desk buying guide: seven things to check Height range, motors, stability, capacity and a few details that store photos do not show. A standing desk is one of the most expensive pieces of a workspace, and store photos make them all look alike. The real differences are in the numbers on the specification sheet. Check these seven things before you buy.  1. Height range, against your body This is the most important number. The desk’s lowest height must suit you seated and its highest must suit you standing. Compare both with your own elbow height (see our desk height guide). For very tall or short people, this alone can rule a desk out. Remember that the desktop’s thickness adds to the frame height. 2. Two-stage or three-stage legs Three-stage legs have three nested columns and usually offer a wider height range than two-stage legs. If you are around average height, two-stage legs may be entirely sufficient. 3. One motor or two On dual-motor desks each leg has its own motor. This generally gives a higher lifting capacity and smoother movement. Single-motor desks are simpler, but compare their capacity and speed carefully on the specification sheet. 4. Lifting capacity Add up everything on the desk: monitors, monitor arm, computer, speakers and the desktop itself. That total should sit comfortably below the stated capacity. 5. Stability at full height Every desk wobbles a little more at its highest setting, but how much varies between models. Foot depth, the frame and crossbars all play a part. If you can, read independent reviews about wobble at standing height; photos do not show it. 6. Desktop size Depth matters more than it seems. To keep a monitor 50 cm away you need enough depth or a monitor arm. Check the width against your room and the number of screens. 7. Everyday details Memory presets, to switch between two heights with one button. Collision detection, which stops the desk if it hits something on the way down. Noise and speed, where the specification sheet states them. Warranty terms for motors, frame and desktop, which often differ. Delivery and return terms; the desk is heavy. Finally, a standing desk is not for standing all day. Read our guide to using a standing desk as well.

title: Monitor arm buying guide: VESA, weight and mounting
sub: Three things to measure first so the arm fits both your monitor and your desk.
text: Monitor arm buying guide: VESA, weight and mounting Three things to measure first so the arm fits both your monitor and your desk. A monitor arm frees your desk and lets you put the screen at exactly the right height and distance: the top at or slightly below eye level, as OSHA recommends. But an arm that does not match your monitor or desk either will not mount or will not hold the screen.  1. The VESA pattern on the monitor Most monitors have four screw holes on the back at a standard spacing called the VESA pattern. The most common patterns for desktop monitors are 75 × 75 and 100 × 100 mm. Check your monitor’s specifications. If it has no VESA holes at all, look for an adapter made for that model. 2. Monitor weight, without its stand Most arms use a gas spring designed for a specific weight range. Find the monitor’s weight without its stand on the specification sheet. If it is heavier than the maximum it will sink; if it is lighter than the minimum it will drift up. Curved and ultrawide monitors are often heavier and need a suitable arm. Check the supported screen size too. 3. The desk edge: clamp or grommet Arms usually fix with a clamp on the desk edge or with a bolt through a cable grommet hole. Measure your desktop thickness and compare it with the clamp’s range. There must be room behind the desk for the clamp, and the desktop must be strong enough to take the load; be careful with glass or very thin tops. Other points Reach: can the arm bring the screen 50 to 100 cm from you? Height: can the top of the screen reach your eye level, especially with a standing desk? Rotation to portrait, if you read long documents or code. Cable routing inside the arm, for a tidier desk. For two monitors, a dual arm or two single arms; two singles are more flexible. Do you need an arm at all? If your current monitor stand adjusts in height and brings the screen to eye level, an arm may not be essential. Our article “Monitor arm or the original stand?” answers that question.

title: Ergonomic keyboard buying guide: split, tenting and the learning curve
sub: The kinds of ergonomic keyboard, who each suits, and what to expect while adjusting.
text: Ergonomic keyboard buying guide: split, tenting and the learning curve The kinds of ergonomic keyboard, who each suits, and what to expect while adjusting. A standard keyboard pulls your hands together in front of you and turns your forearms fully palm-down. Ergonomic keyboards try to bring your hands closer to what OSHA calls a neutral position: hand, wrist and forearm in one line.  Split keyboards The keys are divided into two halves, either in a single wave-shaped body or in two fully separate pieces. Separate halves can sit at shoulder width so your wrists do not bend outward. The more separation, the more flexibility, and the slightly longer the adjustment period. Tenting On a tented keyboard the middle is higher than the edges, like a low pitched roof. This reduces forearm rotation, because your hands turn slightly towards a handshake position. Front-to-back slope Cornell University’s guidance suggests a negative tilt, with the keyboard sloping slightly away from you. So do not flip out the rear feet. Some ergonomic keyboards include a palm rest designed with the same aim. Take the learning curve seriously Fully split or column-staggered keyboards slow your typing for days or weeks. If your work depends on fast typing, either adjust gradually or start with a one-piece wave keyboard, which changes less. If you type in more than one language Many ergonomic keyboards ship with English legends only. That is fine if you touch-type; otherwise consider keycap stickers or laser engraving. The layout itself is set in your operating system, not by the keyboard. Before you buy Size: do you need a number pad? A smaller keyboard brings the mouse closer. Connection: wireless or wired, and how many devices it pairs with. Programmable keys, if you use shortcuts heavily. Return terms, because keyboard feel is entirely personal.

title: Vertical mice: who they suit and how to choose one
sub: The handshake grip, hand size, left or right hand, and a few days of getting used to it.
text: Vertical mice: who they suit and how to choose one The handshake grip, hand size, left or right hand, and a few days of getting used to it. A standard mouse keeps your palm facing down. To do that, the two forearm bones rotate and cross. A vertical mouse holds your hand in a handshake-like position in which the forearm rotates less.  Who is it for? If your forearm or wrist feels tired after long days of mousing, trying a vertical mouse makes sense. It is not a medical treatment, though. If you have pain, numbness or tingling, see a doctor first. Hand size A vertical mouse should suit your hand. One that is too small makes your fingers curl; one that is too large keeps your hand stretched. Many makers state a hand-size range for each model; measure from your wrist crease to the tip of your middle finger and compare. Left or right hand Unlike many standard mice, a vertical mouse is not symmetrical. If you are left-handed, look for a left-handed version, which not every model offers. Angle and precision Vertical mice come at different angles. A gentler angle is closer to a standard mouse and easier to get used to. For precise work such as design, expect a few days of practice. Move from your forearm rather than only your wrist. Placement matters too Even the best mouse pulls your shoulder forward if it sits far from the keyboard. Keep it beside the keyboard at the same height (see our keyboard and mouse position guide). Check the stated hand-size range. Find a left-handed version if you need one. Give yourself a few days to a week to adjust. Read the return terms.

title: An ergonomic workspace on a small budget: where to start
sub: A buying order from cheap to expensive, and what you can do without buying anything.
text: An ergonomic workspace on a small budget: where to start A buying order from cheap to expensive, and what you can do without buying anything. Ergonomics does not start with the most expensive chair. Most improvements come from rearranging what you own and a few small purchases. This order helps each unit of money do the most good.  1. Free: adjust what you own Set your chair so your feet rest on the floor. Put the screen in front of you, about an arm’s length away. Bring the keyboard close and fold its rear feet. None of this costs anything. 2. Creative and nearly free A box or a few sturdy books under your feet instead of a footrest. A small cushion or rolled towel behind your lower back if the chair has no lumbar support. Books under the monitor or laptop to raise the screen. A phone reminder to get up every half hour. 3. A separate keyboard and mouse If you work on a laptop, this is the cheapest and most effective purchase. With a separate keyboard you can raise the screen without raising your hands too. Cornell University recommends exactly this for sustained laptop use. 4. Raise the screen A laptop stand or monitor arm brings the screen to eye level. On a tight budget, books do the job for now. 5. The chair, then the desk A good chair is a big investment, best made once you know exactly which adjustments you need. A standing desk is usually the most expensive item and the last step. Before either, read the buying guide for that category. One simple rule Buy the thing that solves a specific problem you feel today: a tired neck, wrists or back. Buying several items for one problem, or something only because it looks good, spends your budget without effect.

title: Setting up a workspace in a small room
sub: A shallow desk, a monitor arm, room behind the chair and light: working well in a small corner.
text: Setting up a workspace in a small room A shallow desk, a monitor arm, room behind the chair and light: working well in a small corner. Not everyone has a separate study. Many of us work in a bedroom corner or beside the living room. A small space has limits, but with a few good choices you can still follow the same ergonomic rules.  Desk depth versus monitor distance Shallow desks take less room, but OSHA recommends at least 50 cm between you and the monitor. If the desk is shallow, a monitor arm lets you push the screen back to the rear edge of the desk or slightly beyond. Another option is a laptop on a stand, which takes up less surface. Free up the desk surface In a small space, every centimetre of desk counts. A monitor arm, cables gathered under the desk and a wall shelf above it keep the work surface clear. Do not forget the space behind the chair The chair needs to roll back a little so you can sit and stand comfortably. If there is a wall or a bed behind it, measure that space before buying a desk. Light in a small space If you can, place the desk so the window is to your side. In a dark corner, a desk lamp or monitor light bar is needed so the screen is not the only light. When the desk is shared If several people share a desk, a chair with quick height adjustment matters more. A standing desk with memory presets stores each person’s height. A folding laptop stand and a compact keyboard can be packed away after work.

title: Tidying desk cables, especially on a standing desk
sub: A cable tray, a route down the leg and one key point: slack for when the desk rises.
text: Tidying desk cables, especially on a standing desk A cable tray, a route down the leg and one key point: slack for when the desk rises. Messy cables do not just look bad. On a standing desk, a cable that is too short gets pulled when the desk rises and can drag a device off the desk or be damaged. Tidying cables is an afternoon’s work.  1. First, take stock Unplug everything and see where each cable goes. Set aside any you do not use. There are usually more cables than you think. 2. Put the power strip under the desk Fit a cable tray under the desk and put the power strip in it. Every device then draws power from under the desk, and only one cable runs from the tray down to the wall socket. 3. One route to the floor Run the main cable down beside a desk leg. Spiral wraps or a cable spine gather several cables into one route. 4. Slack for a standing desk The most important point: raise the desk to its highest setting and see which cables pull tight. Every cable running from the desk to the floor or wall must still have some slack at full height. Keep cables clear of the moving legs and frame. 5. On the desk, one cable each For each device on the desk, bring one cable up over the back edge. Reusable hook-and-loop ties make later changes easy. Safety Do not load power strips and adapters beyond their rating. Keep cables away from chair casters and the desk’s moving parts. Do not enclose warm power adapters where air cannot reach them.
